parameters.name: shoe_type
parameters.description: Categories of men's shoes with their characteristics, formality, and appropriate contexts

values.definition: Closed lacing (Balmoral). Most formal shoe. Two narrow rows of stitching with a round or slightly square plain toe, sometimes with a medallion decoration. Beveled waist enhances elegance. The basis shoe style for smart, tailored town wear. Black is de rigueur for formal occasions.

Oxford with perforated toecap decoration (broguing) but no wing. Stylistically midway between plain Oxford and full brogue — not as formal as sleek Oxford, not as rustic as full brogue. Good match for softer or patterned suiting fabrics like flannel or Prince of Wales check.

Oxford with perforations and curved toecap extending back in a W shape (wingtip). Bulkier, less formal than plain cap-toe. Larger proportions allow a more robust match with flannels, cheviots, or tweeds. Called 'Budapests' in continental Europe. In brown, ideal for informal wear with tweed and country suits.

Open lacing — sides sewn on top of the vamp. Less formal than Oxford due to open throat. Suitable for those not compelled to wear elegant Oxfords. In caramel brown, popular in southern Europe with flannel pants and navy blazers. Also goes well with corduroy and jeans.

Buckle closure instead of laces. Halfway between formal lace-up and casual loafer. Superbly proportioned symmetry. Can be found in plain toe or brogued. Black calf to brown reversed calf, from dressy to casual. Particularly popular in France. Best with slim-cut pants that don't catch on the buckle.

Slip-on with cross-strap on instep. Named because 1950s Ivy League students put pennies under the strap for luck. Bass Weejuns are the classic. Shape said to originate from Norwegian fishermen's shoes. Less formal than any lace-up. Originally seen as 'going out in slippers.'

Loafer with decorative leather tassels on instep. Often compared to navy blue blazer — equally versatile and hard to classify. Alden claims credit for the modern design. Popular in southern Europe with dark suits as business wear. English makers cut them higher than American originals.

Horsebit loafer with gilt snaffle decoration. One of a handful of timeless classics regarded worldwide as a badge of good taste. Can be worn with English corduroy, rough tweed, cashmere, khaki shorts, jeans, or even a tuxedo. Three pairs in black and brown can hold their own against a whole shoe cupboard of welted shoes.

Ankle boot with elastic side panels. Originally designed by Queen Victoria's boot maker J. Sparkes Hall. The elastic allows a trimly fitted ankle without laces. Traditionally bespoke style. A well-heeled loafer aficionado's champion of this traditional style.

Ankle boot with two or three eyelets, named after the chukka period in polo. Often unlined. Can be found in smooth tan calfskin or suede. Fitted with Tyrolean crepe or rubber sole. Traditionally attired toff in brown leather with lug sole — the dress-down urbanite.

Slip-on evening shoe, often with silk bow or monogram. Patent leather or velvet. For formal evening wear (white tie, black tie) and home entertaining. Albert slipper with embroidered motifs for smoking jacket wear. Cecil Beaton made these famous as an evening staple.

White buckskin Oxford with red rubber sole. American preppy staple. Perfect companion to the khaki pant or madras Bermuda shorts. More relaxed style than American white bucks — character so charismatic it can be in their understated manner. Summer and resort wear.

Two-tone shoe, originally designed in brown willow calf and white buck or reverse calf suede. Also known as 'co-respondent' in England (associated with characters who acted as correspondents in divorce cases). Unusual contrast of texture. Holiday and sport wardrobe essential.
Sperry Topsiders are the classic. Originally designed for sailing — non-slip sole. Popular with landlubbers as well. Casual summer/weekend shoe. Goes with shorts, chinos, jeans.

parameters.name: shoe_lacing_system
parameters.description: The fundamental construction distinction that determines shoe formality

values.definition: Sides sewn under the vamp, closing over a separate tongue. More formal — feet look more 'dressed.' All Oxfords have closed lacing. Called 'Balmorals' or 'Bals' in America.

Sides sewn on top of the vamp, which extends backward to form the tongue. Less formal — more give over the instep, making them slightly more comfortable. Called 'Bluchers' in America, 'Derbys' in England/Europe.

parameters.notes: Closed lacing is always more formal than open lacing in the same shoe style.

parameters.name: shoe_leather_type
parameters.description: The leather material used for shoe uppers, affecting formality, texture, and care

values.definition: Standard material for quality men's shoes. Fine grain, takes a high polish. Brown calfskin acquires an antiqued patina over time — changing highlights like light placed on a polished mahogany tabletop. Black calfskin is the formal standard.

Brushed/napped leather with soft matte texture. First appeared at the 1924 International Polo match. Initially considered a breach of good taste by many. Brown suede can be worn year-round and suits well with tweeds and country combinations. Shifts any shoe shape toward casual.

Shell leather from the hindquarters of a horse. Very rare and expensive. Distinctive deep, rich color with a waxy luster. Exceptionally durable. Well-established in the USA for many years. Only recently gaining awareness in Europe.
Highly polished, glossy finish leather. Required for formal evening wear (white tie). Also appropriate for black tie. Pumps or Oxfords in patent are the most formal shoe option.

Crocodile or alligator leather. In a dark honey tone, affords the normally meek-shod man a rare opportunity to express himself in sybaritic sheen. Whether in a monk-strap for the weekend or plain cap-toe for the office, exotic leather elevates any shoe model.

parameters.name: shoe_color_rule
parameters.description: Rules for matching shoe color to outfit, one of the most fundamental dressing principles

values.definition: Black shoes for formal and business formal wear. De rigueur with dark navy or charcoal suits. Required for all evening formal wear. Black will always lack the antiqued brown's patina and changing highlights.

Dark antique brown accepted with dark blue suits since the 1930s. Esquire in 1936: 'At the present time, dark brown shoes are considered correct and satisfactory for wear with a dark blue suit.' Brown shoes invest any dressier surroundings with a patina of antiqued charm.

Lighter browns suitable for tweed, country, and casual wear. Light tan shoes not considered appropriate with dark business suits. Shaded for light-colored spring clothing, and rich in tone for darker worsteds.
Rich wine tones. Versatile — works with both dark formal and casual ensembles. Bass Weejuns in burgundy are a classic. Cordovan shoes often come in this distinctive shade.

parameters.name: hosiery_type
parameters.description: Types of socks and their role in connecting the trouser to the shoe

values.definition: Fine gauge, over-the-calf. Should match the trouser rather than the shoe — creating an unbroken vertical line from trouser to footwear. Navy socks appear richer than black with a dark suit. Patterned hose help integrate the top and bottom halves of the ensemble. Silk dress hosiery for formal evening wear.

Argyle, clocked, striped, or small-patterned socks. The hose's most frequent stage partner is the necktie — it is the next most visible flash of color and pattern. Patterned hose promote harmony between different sectors of an outfit when the necktie motif appears in fine gauge within dress hosiery.

Heavier gauge. Anklet or half-length. The bulkier the trouser, the heavier the hose. Wool socks with wide chunked flannel trousers. For shorts, the anklet is still the most chic way to maintain bare ankles. Thick argyle socks with tweed jackets for country wear.

parameters.notes: General principle: the sock should match the trouser rather than the shoe. Black sock with a dark navy suit should be avoided — navy or dark gray is richer. Bare ankle (no-show) only with shorts or very casual summer wear.

parameters.name: pocket_handkerchief_type
parameters.description: Types of pocket squares and their display methods — one of the few remaining personal expression accessories

values.definition: The most versatile and essential. Always available as fallback. Points neither too even nor too sharpened with a rolling iron. Best size is about a 16-inch square. Hand-stitched rolled edges. Starched white provides a crisp counterpoint to the dark suit. Most formal pocket square option.

Should echo a color in the necktie, shirt, or jacket — but never exactly match the tie (a sure sign of an unsophisticated dresser). A solid colored handkerchief can only be trusted with a patterned necktie. If the hank color and pattern usually determine its choice.

Printed or woven pattern. Should coordinate with but not match the necktie. Ideally a foulard hank contains colors found in both the shirt and tie. Contrast in textures helps keep them from appearing too matched — a silk square with a tweed jacket creates appealing contrast.

parameters.name: pocket_square_fold
parameters.description: Methods of displaying the pocket handkerchief, each conveying different levels of formality and personality

values.definition: Flat, horizontal fold showing a clean rectangle of fabric above the pocket. The most formal and understated display. Called 'TV fold' because American TV anchors adopted it in the 1960s. Sharp, purposeful appearance but can look too stiff.

Casual, rounded puff of fabric. Most informal display. Cary Cooper and the Duke of Windsor favored this approach — nubbed and happily curled up with casually askew ties. Should rest in the breast pocket at a jaunty angle.

One or more points showing above the pocket, angled toward the shoulder. Positioning reinforces the diagonal line of the jacket's lapel and accentuates the chest's V shape and shoulder's breadth. The Duke's points leaned customarily toward one corner.

parameters.notes: The most important thing is that deployment should appear untutored — casual aplomb. Like the tying of a bow tie, the most important thing is that it should not appear too deliberate.

parameters.name: belt_type
parameters.description: Types of belts and their role in the outfit — the transition piece between upper and lower halves

values.definition: Constructed of single-ply fine-grained leather in 1 to 1.25-inch width. Buckle should be simple — silver or gold depending on the color of your jewelry. Smooth calfskin or baby crocodile/alligator. When buckled, the end should finish between the first and second belt loop. Never mix leather colors — brown belt with black shoe is a violation.

Wider, more textured. Suede, woven leather, canvas, or D-ring buckle styles. The Duke of Windsor used a gilded D-ring buckle to dress down into a semi-sport belt that accorded with his patterned ensembles' informality. More contrast between belt and trouser = more casual.

parameters.notes: Belt color should match shoe color. The less contrast between belt and trouser, the more elegant the effect. Dress belts should be dulled leather with understated buckle. Belts should never be worn with suspenders.

parameters.name: suspender_brace_type
parameters.description: Types of braces/suspenders — the superior trouser support system for pleated trousers

values.definition: The proper type. Attach to buttons on the inside or outside of the trouser waistband. Six buttons total: two rear (centered on back seam), four front (two near center and two just forward of side seam). Suspenders allow the natural pull of gravity to keep the pants' front taut and crease knife-like. Albert Thurston still makes the Rolls-Royce of trouser braces.
Attach with metal clips. Probably acceptable for farm work but not under a suit of clothes. Considered the lowest tier of suspender. Can damage fine trouser waistbands.

parameters.notes: Width should be 1.25 to 1.5 inches — narrower and they bind, wider and they are uncomfortable. Belts and suspenders should never be worn together; belt loops should not appear on suspender-equipped trousers. Braces should be concealed under a jacket — exposed braces are a source of embarrassment per Oscar Wilde.

parameters.name: brace_aesthetics
parameters.description: How to coordinate suspender colors and patterns with the rest of the outfit

values.definition: Since braces share the same vertical plane as the tie, these two are coordinated first. Solid or simple striped ribbon can pick up one of the tie's colors without competing with the tie's design. A solid pair affords more versatility than a patterned pair.

Patterned braces coordinate better with solid or striped neckwear. They can either repeat one of the tie's colors or look to the trouser or shirt for companionship. Since suspenders are hidden under vest or jacket, they enjoy freedom to complement all or none of the torso's accessories.

parameters.name: cufflink_type
parameters.description: Types of cufflinks for French cuff shirts — one of the few opportunities for a man to display personal jewelry

values.definition: The most prized type — two decorative faces connected by a chain or link. Both sides bear design and lineage. Wearing cuff links that clip on one side exposes the superstructure and suggests you could afford only the cheapest version.
Fabric knots in various colors. Casual and playful. Good for everyday French cuff wear when formal jewelry would be excessive.

A proper dress set includes sided cuff links, two or three matching shirt studs, and no fewer than three waistcoat buttons. Gold for daytime; colored stones for evening. Colored rubies, emeralds, or sapphires are too flashy for day wear and reserved for after-dark elegance.

parameters.name: tie_accessory_type
parameters.description: Accessories that interact with the necktie — functional and decorative

values.definition: An American invention. Adds a touch of elan and eccentric charm when canted slightly downward. Prevents the tie from flipping in the breeze or acting as a napkin while dining. Affixing the tie to the shirt front helps maintain the tie's arch and measure of panache. Should be simple and understated.
Pins the shirt collar points under the tie knot, lifting the knot and creating an elegant arch. Adds a 3D sculptural quality to the neckwear presentation. Requires pin-collar or eyelet-collar shirts.

parameters.name: watch_timepiece_type
parameters.description: Types of timepieces and their formality implications

values.definition: Thin, elegant case that fits under a shirt cuff. Gold or steel. Leather strap for formal; metal bracelet acceptable for business. Oversize watches impede the closing of the shirt cuff. The slimmer and more discreet, the more formal. Thick diver-style watches are too large for formal wear.

Required with a waistcoat or formal evening dress (white tie, black tie). A thin dress pocket watch is deemed appropriate for black and white etiquette. The pocket watch achieved peak popularity during the 1930s as the uniform accessory of well-dressed men.

parameters.notes: Oversized wristwatches do not hide well for the man's overall style and encumber bracelets invariably accelerate the fraying of the shirt's cuff.

parameters.name: boutonniere_type
parameters.description: The lapel flower — a small grace note of male refinement

values.definition: The best flowers are those that provide a flat button of color — like the carnation or cornflower. The small carnation's base can sit in the buttonhole without its stem having to be threaded through the lapel guard. Not so large as to overwhelm the average-width lapel. Red carnation for an afternoon wedding is the standard.
Small, flat, deeply colored. Traditional gentleman's flower. Like the hidden collar button, the stem should be invisible — concealed behind the lapel.

parameters.notes: A man can wear both a pocket handkerchief and a boutonniere — this is not gilding the lily. The lapel buttonhole was made to accommodate a flower. The stem should be invisible. Pinning a flower to the outside of the lapel makes you look like an usher at a wedding.

parameters.name: hat_type
parameters.description: Categories of men's hats, their formality, and appropriate contexts

values.definition: The most formal hat. Black silk. Only worn with morning dress or evening dress (tails). Required at Royal Ascot. Takes a certain sense of style to wear properly. Legend has it that it debuted on January 15, 1797 when hat-maker John Hetherington first wore one in the street.

Named after the German spa town Bad Homburg, discovered by King Edward VII. Second in formality only to the top hat (leaving bowler aside as an English specialty). A dented crown with a stiff brim turned up all around. Goes with formal day wear.

Rigid, dome-shaped hat. Designed in Lock's workshop for gamekeepers — offered little purchase to obstructions. Symbol of London stockbrokers until 1960s. Now worn only by Queen's Guards officers in civilian dress. Called 'derby' in America, 'chapeau melon' in French. More eccentric than practical today.

Classic gentleman's hat with soft brim that can be worn turned up or down. More elegant than trilby thanks to broader brim, but more casual than bowler or Homburg. The hat par excellence for most men. At greatest risk of falling into oblivion — no clear niche left in modern dress.

Brown trilby is the insignia of the horse-racing fraternity. Crumpled brown felt, narrow hatband with bow on left side. Obligatory at English equestrian events. Also exists as a collapsible hat that fits in a pocket.

Woven from jipijapa palm leaves in Ecuador (despite the name). Light, lightproof summer hat. The 'optimo crown' (with crest) is the classic original — can be folded without damage. Summer classic since the Panama Canal era. Popular at Wimbledon. Like a good cigar — not everybody's cup of tea but devotees grow extremely fond of it.

Soft-brimmed hat in tweed fabric. Worn whenever a tweed jacket or suit is appropriate — weekends, traveling, country sports. Favored by men of intellect and science. Goes best with informal but traditional overcoats — duffel coat, British Warm, reversible coats, Barbours.

Sporting headgear through and through. Only caps from Great Britain have the authentic flat cut. Mainly worn in the country for shooting, riding, or fishing. Also includes the deerstalker (check pattern) and Tirolean (green, favored by walkers).
Round, rigid straw hat. Originally favored headgear of English butchers. In the 1920s became a universal summer hat. Today hardly ever seen except at the Henley rowing regatta.

Modern classic slowly infiltrating the most elevated circles. Quintessentially American peaked cap that has crept into classic sportswear. May possibly pave the way for a broader comeback of headwear. Casual/athletic only.

parameters.name: necktie_type
parameters.description: Categories of neckties by construction and material — from Roetzel's dedicated chapter

values.definition: The standard. Cut in three sections on the bias (45 degrees to weave) per Jesse Langsdorf's 1924 patent. Most good neckties still made this way. Self-tipping (tips lined with the tie's own fabric) is an Italian hallmark. Charvet of Paris offers the world's largest range of woven silk ties. A Hermes necktie is one of the safest sartorial investments.

A square piece of silk folded seven times into necktie shape with no interlining — 100% silk. The non plus ultra of tiemaking and the ultimate in understatement. Volume comes entirely from folded silk. Very expensive. Rare masterpiece of the necktie maker's art.

Diagonal stripes in club, regimental, college, or school colors. In England, wearing the wrong club tie can be a serious faux pas if the Englishman you're meeting belongs to that club. English stripes run left-down-to-right; American 'rep' ties run the opposite direction.

Made of pure wool, cashmere, or blends. Warmer and softer than silk. Doesn't form the crisp formality of silk but has its place. Particularly appropriate for fall/winter with tweed and flannel. Popular in academic circles. Nicky of Milan makes particularly exquisite versions. Knitted wool varieties for a square-end casual look.

Knitted construction rather than woven. Usually square-ended. The formal version is black or dark blue, same width as ordinary tie, perfectly correct with a dark gray suit. Simplicity calls for a sure hand in combining with the right shirt. Similar following to academics, artists, writers, journalists.

Self-tied is the only correct form for both formal wear and everyday wear. Pre-tied bows are instantly recognizable and considered inferior. Required in white for white tie; required in black for black tie. Available in silk, cotton pique (for formal), and novelty fabrics.

parameters.name: ring_type
parameters.description: Types of finger rings appropriate for men — the most discreet form of personal jewelry

values.definition: Simple platinum or gold band on the ring finger. By mid-twentieth century, nearly 80% of American brides had revived the old-world custom of wearing bands. The simple wedding band or dress ring is normally sufficient — younger men should stick to this.

Family crest or initials engraved. Can be worn on either hand. The signet ring was historically used to notarize documents with one's own seal. Organizational, class, or fraternity rings can also be worn. Multiple conspicuous rings have been considered gaudy and associated with men who 'make a living by exploiting others.'

garment_taxonomy_principles.name: shoe_formality_hierarchy
garment_taxonomy_principles.description: Patent pump > plain cap-toe Oxford (closed) > half-brogue > full-brogue wingtip > Derby/Blucher > monkstrap > tassel loafer > penny loafer > moccasin. Closed lacing is always more formal than open lacing. Broguing (perforations) always reduces formality. Suede leather always shifts one tier more casual than polished leather in the same style.

garment_taxonomy_principles.name: sock_matches_trouser_not_shoe
garment_taxonomy_principles.description: Hosiery should match the trouser rather than the shoe — perceiving them from the leg bottom as a unit. Stopping the eye at the ankle by blocking it with a clashing sock creates a break in the visual line. Patterned hose help integrate top and bottom halves of the ensemble.

garment_taxonomy_principles.name: pocket_square_never_matches_tie
garment_taxonomy_principles.description: A matching handkerchief and necktie is not only a sign of an unsure dresser but also a sure way to lead the eye across the body and away from the face. A solid pocket hank should echo a color in the necktie but never duplicate it in fabric or exact color.

garment_taxonomy_principles.name: accessories_as_personal_expression
garment_taxonomy_principles.description: Since Victorian times, well-dressed men have tended to afford all but the most discreet and understated accessories. The money clip, tie clip, collar pin, key chain, wristwatch, and cuff links are utilitarian, not decorative. However, a man can still wear a little bit of gold taste. Accessories are like local cuisine — they hold their own against international standardization.

garment_taxonomy_principles.name: hat_formality_hierarchy
garment_taxonomy_principles.description: Top hat > Homburg > bowler > fedora > trilby > Panama/boater > tweed hat > flat cap > baseball cap. The hat has largely lost its everyday function but remains required for formal occasions (morning dress, evening dress). In England, hats are still expected at horse racing and equestrian events.

garment_taxonomy_principles.name: three_pairs_minimum
garment_taxonomy_principles.description: Three pairs of welted shoes are sufficient as a basic collection: one pair of brown brogues, one of black Oxfords, and one of monkstraps or loafers. Then add light moccasins and boat shoes. Shoes should have at least a day or two to recover after every wearing. But few men who acquire a taste for shoes will make do with the minimum.

cross_domain_intersections.name: shoes_x_occasion
cross_domain_intersections.description: Shoe type must match the occasion from Domain 7. Patent pumps for white tie. Black Oxfords for business formal and morning dress. Brown brogues for country and smart casual. Loafers for business casual. Boat shoes for weekend only. Mismatching shoe formality to occasion is one of the most visible dressing errors.

cross_domain_intersections.name: shoes_x_fabric
cross_domain_intersections.description: Shoe texture should relate to outfit fabric texture from Domain 8. Polished calfskin with smooth worsted. Suede with flannel and tweed. Full brogues with textured country fabrics. Half-brogues bridge formal and informal fabrics like Prince of Wales check.

cross_domain_intersections.name: accessories_x_color
cross_domain_intersections.description: Pocket square, socks, and belt colors interact with the color system from Domain 3. Belt matches shoes. Socks match trousers. Pocket square echoes but never duplicates tie. These coordination rules create visual coherence across the full outfit.

cross_domain_intersections.name: hat_x_occasion_outfit
cross_domain_intersections.description: Hat type maps to both occasion (Domain 7) and outfit style. Top hat only with tails. Trilby with tweed at races. Panama for summer events. Flat cap for country sports. Fedora for smart everyday wear. The hat must harmonize with the outfit's overall formality and fabric texture.
